reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: A segment of an epicardial coronary artery, usually the mid left anterior descending, dips into the myocardium and is compressed during systole
Angiography shows systolic narrowing that relaxes in diastole, the milking effect, since most coronary perfusion occurs in diastole
The overwhelming majority are benign incidental findings with a favourable natural history
Symptomatic cases may report exertional chest pain, and rarely arrhythmia or ischaemic events are attributed to deep or long bridges
Diastolic flow disturbance and a persistent early-diastolic delay in relaxation can occasionally impair perfusion
Tachycardia shortens diastole and can unmask or worsen symptoms by reducing perfusion time
Most patients need reassurance only; medical therapy that reduces contractility and heart rate is first-line, with intervention reserved for refractory, well-documented ischaemia
reference.pathophysiology: Myocardial bridging occurs when a portion of an epicardial coronary artery, most often the mid left anterior descending, takes an intramuscular course so that overlying myocardium compresses it during systole. Because coronary perfusion is predominantly diastolic, the systolic compression is usually of little consequence, which explains why most bridges are benign. In deeper or longer bridges the compression can persist into early diastole and a phase lag in vessel re-expansion may transiently reduce flow, and tachycardia further curtails diastolic filling time. Local wall stress at the bridge entrance may also predispose the proximal segment to atherosclerosis. The net functional effect ranges from none in the great majority to occasional demand ischaemia in a minority.
additionalDifferentials: Anomalous coronary artery origin or course
additionalInvestigations: Coronary angiography demonstrating systolic compression with diastolic relaxation
Coronary CT angiography showing the intramyocardial segment
Intravascular imaging or physiological indices to assess functional significance in selected cases
Stress testing or perfusion imaging to document inducible ischaemia
redFlags: Documented exertional ischaemia attributable to a deep or long bridge
Ventricular arrhythmia associated with the bridged segment
Persistent symptoms despite optimal rate and contractility control
Ischaemic event in a young patient without atherosclerotic risk factors
reference.prognosis: The natural history is generally benign with normal life expectancy in the majority; adverse events are rare and largely confined to deep, long bridges or those with proven ischaemia.
pitfalls: Overtreating an incidental bridge and attributing unrelated chest pain to it
Using nitrates, which can worsen systolic compression and symptoms
Failing to control heart rate, allowing tachycardia to shorten diastolic perfusion time
Ignoring coexisting fixed atherosclerotic disease proximal to the bridge
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children and Adolescents
management: Reassure and observe the majority, who have a benign incidental bridge requiring no treatment
Use negative chronotropic and inotropic agents, beta-blockers or non-dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers, as first-line therapy for symptomatic ischaemia to prolong diastolic perfusion time
Avoid nitrates and pure vasodilators, which can accentuate systolic compression and worsen symptoms
Address atherosclerotic risk factors, as the segment proximal to the bridge is prone to plaque formation
Reserve surgical myotomy (unroofing) or coronary bypass for refractory symptoms with documented ischaemia
Investigate persistent symptoms with stress or perfusion imaging and intracoronary physiological indices to confirm functional significance
